Records

Manning holds a number of individual NFL career records:

  • Most AP NFL Most Valuable Player Awards: 5 (2003, 2004, 2008, 2009, 2013)
  • Most First-Team All-Pro selections for a quarterback: 7 (2003–2005, 2008–2009, 2012–2013)[13]
  • First quarterback to reach 200 career wins (playoffs and regular season)[457]
  • Most touchdown passes, season: 55 (2013)[17]
  • Most seasons with at least 4,000 passing yards: 14 (1999–2004, 2006–2010, 2012–2014)[458]
  • Most passing yards, season: 5,477 (2013)[16]
  • Yards per game in a single season: 342.3 (2013) (tied with Drew Brees)[459]
  • Most NFL teams beaten: 32 (tied with Brett Favre, Drew Brees, and Tom Brady)[460]
  • Most consecutive seasons with at least 25 touchdown passes: 13 (1998–2010)[458]
  • Most games with a perfect passer rating, career: 4 (includes 1 playoff game) (tied with Ben Roethlisberger and Lamar Jackson)[197]
  • Most consecutive games started to open a career: 208[110][461]
  • Most consecutive games with at least 2 touchdown passes: 15 (2013–2014)[462]
  • Most consecutive games with at least 4 touchdown passes: 5 (games 7–11, 2004)[463]
  • Most games with at least four touchdown passes, season: 9 (2013)[463]
  • Only quarterback with at least six touchdown passes in three games[464]
  • One of eight quarterbacks with at least seven touchdown passes in a game[465]
  • Highest completion percentage by a quarterback in one month in NFL history (min. 75 attempts): 81.8% (December 2008)[110]
  • Most consecutive regular season wins as a starter: 23 (2008–2009)[466]
  • Only quarterback to lead five consecutive 4th-quarter comeback wins (games 7–11, 2009)[467]
  • One of four quarterbacks to defeat the other 31 teams during the regular season[468]
  • Most interceptions thrown by a rookie quarterback: 28[469]

Personal life

Manning was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, the second son of Olivia (née Williams) and former NFL quarterback Archie Manning. His younger brother is two-time Super Bowl champion Eli Manning.[470] Some have described the Mannings as football's "royal family."[471][472]

Manning married his wife, Ashley, in Memphis on St. Patrick's Day, 2001.[473] A graduate of the University of Virginia, Ashley was introduced to him by her parents' next-door neighbor the summer before Manning's freshman year in college. The couple has twins: a son, Marshall Williams, and a daughter, Mosley Thompson, who were born on March 31, 2011.[474] They live in Denver, Colorado.[475][476] Upon his arrival in Denver, Manning temporarily lived in a house owned by Mike Shanahan until purchasing his own home for $4.575 million.[477][478]

Manning is a Presbyterian Christian. At age 13, he said, "I committed my life to Christ, and that faith has been most important to me ever since." Manning said his priorities ranked in order are "...faith, family, friends, and football." Manning said he prays every night and before games and added, "I hope (and pray) I don't do too many things that displease Him before I get to Heaven myself. I believe, too, that life is much better and freer when you're committed to God in that way."[479][480]

Manning reportedly memorized the Colts' playbook within a week after being drafted,[101] and in 2012, he was able to precisely recall the details and timing of a specific play that he used at Tennessee 16 years earlier.[481]

During the summer, Archie, Peyton, Eli, and oldest sibling Cooper run the Manning Passing Academy, a five-day camp that aims to improve the offensive skills of quarterbacks, wide receivers, tight ends, and running backs.[482] In addition to the Mannings, the camp has included many prominent football players as coaches, such as Colts wide receivers Marvin Harrison and Reggie Wayne.[483]

Manning, along with his father Archie, co-authored a book titled Manning: A Father, His Sons, and a Football Legacy, which was released in 2000. The book covers Archie's and Cooper's lives and careers, and Manning's life and career up to the time that the book was released, and examines football from both Archie's and Manning's points-of-view.[484] Manning wrote about Jamie Ann Naughright, who accused him of sexual harassment, stating that she had a "vulgar mouth." He described his conduct toward her as "crude, maybe, but harmless."[485][486][487][488] Naughright sued for defamation, resulting in an undisclosed settlement in 2003 and a court order imposing a condition on both Manning and Naughright preventing them from ever talking about the settlement or each other again.[486][488][489]

Mark Kiszla, a sports columnist for the Denver Post, in a column about Manning's future plans, said that Manning's net worth "is estimated to be in excess of $150 million" and "That's not enough money to buy an NFL franchise by himself, although an ownership group that included Manning as president with a financial stake in the team would be led by a brilliant football mind."[490] He has donated over $8,000 to Republican politicians, among them Fred Thompson, Bob Corker, and former President George W. Bush.[491] During the 2016 presidential race, Manning contributed to the campaign of Jeb Bush.[492] On October 26, 2012, Manning bought 21 Papa John's Pizza stores, all in Colorado.[493] He sold his shares of the stores in February 2018.[494]

During his professional career, Manning earned the nickname, "the Sheriff". The nickname had its origin traced to a Monday Night Football broadcast in 2009 when analyst Jon Gruden described Manning's ability to use audibles at the line of scrimmage on the road.[495]

In honor of Manning, the University of Tennessee offers a Peyton Manning Scholarship to incoming freshmen.[496]

Other work

Manning has been credited with helping to improve the city of Indianapolis.[497][498][499][500] A curator at the Indiana State Museum stated that "There is no Super Bowl held here without Peyton. There is no Lucas Oil Stadium without Peyton. Without Peyton, the Colts would probably be in L.A. right now."[501][502] He became one of the NFL's most marketable players, appearing in several television and printed advertisements for some of the NFL's biggest sponsors.[503][504]

On March 24, 2007, his 31st birthday, Manning hosted NBC's Saturday Night Live (season 32, episode 16).[505] His brother Eli also hosted the show five years later. The episode earned the show's highest household rating in more than 10 months in the metered markets.[506] He appeared on SNL again in 2008, the Saturday Night Live 40th Anniversary Special in 2015,[507] and on Weekend Update on the January 29, 2022, episode hosted by Willem Dafoe.[508]

On May 27, 2007, Manning waved the green flag to begin the 91st Indianapolis 500.[509] On February 18, 2018, he drove the pace car during the 2018 Daytona 500.[510] Before the latter, he made a guest appearance on Fox NASCAR's pre-race show alongside race pole-sitter and fellow Nationwide Insurance spokesman Alex Bowman.[511]

In 2009, Manning guest voiced (with his brothers Eli and Cooper) on an episode of The Simpsons called "O Brother, Where Bart Thou?" in which Bart dreams of having a baby brother and sees famous brothers like The Marx Brothers, The Blues Brothers, The Wright Brothers, The Mario Brothers, and The Manning Brothers.[512] He also voiced Guapo in the 2017 movie Ferdinand.[513]

Manning hosted the 2017 ESPY Awards on July 12, 2017.[514]

Manning is the host of Peyton's Places, a documentary series about football on ESPN+, in which Manning interviews players, coaches, and celebrities. The series was renewed for a third season in December 2020.[515][516] The series is currently produced by Manning's own production studio, Omaha Productions, which he co-founded in 2020 and is named after his trademark audible call.[517] Through the studio, Manning also serves as a producer on the sports documentary series Quarterback and Full Court Press.[518][519]

In 2021, Peyton hosted a revival of the quiz show College Bowl, with his brother Cooper as his "sidekick".[520] The series was renewed in 2022 for a second season.[521]

In 2021, Peyton and Eli began hosting an alternative broadcast of Monday Night Football called the Manningcast on ESPN2 and ESPN+.[522] The show features segments with special guest stars from entertainment, politics, and sports while the Manning brothers watch and commentate on the game.[523]

Manning has also expressed interest in becoming a potential owner of the Denver Broncos.[524][525][526][527]

In 2023, it was announced Manning would join the University of Tennessee as a professor in the College of Communication and Information.[528] Most recently, his Omaha Productions company had secured a deal with 20th Television.[529]

On June 3, 2025, it was announced Manning would be joining the ownership group of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) team Denver Summit FC.[530][531] Manning had a supporting role as Laird in the 2025 movie Is This Thing On? which was directed by Bradley Cooper with Will Arnett as the lead.[532]

Philanthropy

Shortly after beginning his NFL career, Manning started his own charity called the Peyback Foundation. The Peyback Foundation's mission is to help disadvantaged kids, and focuses its efforts in Louisiana, Tennessee, Indiana, and Colorado.[533][534][535] For his work with the foundation, Manning received the Samuel S. Beard Award for Greatest Public Service by an Individual 35 Years or Under, which is given out annually by Jefferson Awards.[536]

Manning, along with his brother Eli, volunteered their assistance in the wake of Hurricane Katrina. Among the tasks performed, the Mannings assisted in the delivery of 30,000 pounds of water, Gatorade, baby formula, diapers, and pillows to the people of New Orleans.[537]

In September 2007, St. Vincent Hospital in Indianapolis renamed its children's hospital to Peyton Manning Children's Hospital at St. Vincent. Manning and his wife made a donation of an undisclosed amount to St. Vincent's and have a relationship with the hospital since he came to Indianapolis.[538][539]

In 2022, the Peyback foundation teamed up with Georgia Tech to launch a scholarship in honor of Manning's former Broncos teammate Demaryius Thomas.[540] The foundation also launched scholarships at six historically black colleges and universities.[541]

In 2024, Manning was honored with the Mizel Institute Community Enrichment Award.[542] In 2025, Manning donated $4 million to the University of Tennessee College of Communication and Information.[543]
